title: Closed subgroups of split tori are diagonalizable
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Group schemes and homomorphisms are as in [def-sc-group-scheme], and closed subgroups as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Let $r\geq0$ and let $K\subset\mathbf G_m^r$ be a closed subgroup scheme, where $\mathbf G_m$ is [def-sc-gm-ga], so $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$. There is a finitely generated abelian group $M$ such that $K\simeq D(M)=\operatorname{Spec}F[M]$ as $F$-group schemes [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. The group algebra $F[M]$ has basis $(e_m)_{m\in M}$, multiplication $e_me_n=e_{m+n}$, comultiplication $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$, counit $e_m\mapsto1$ and antipode $e_m\mapsto e_{-m}$, with tensor products as in [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. If $K$ has finite-dimensional coordinate algebra [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], then $M$ is finite. Thus every finite closed subgroup scheme of a split torus is of multiplicative type, meaning diagonalizable after extension to an algebraic closure.

source.place: Theorems 12.8 and 12.9(a),(c), printed pp.233--234; Section 12.14, printed p.236

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-group-geometric-criteria], $D_F(\mathbf Z^r)\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$ with coordinate Hopf algebra $F[\mathbf Z^r]$ and its displayed monomial basis. Apply the affine quotient characterization of a closed immersion in [def-weil-closed-immersion] to $K\hookrightarrow D_F(\mathbf Z^r)$. It gives $K=\operatorname{Spec}B$ and a surjective $F$-algebra map $q:F[\mathbf Z^r]\to B$. By [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf], $B$ has a counital coassociative comultiplication, counit and antipode induced by its group structure. Since the inclusion is a group homomorphism, pulling back its multiplication, identity and inverse compatibility diagrams gives $\Delta_Bq=(q\otimes q)\Delta$, $\varepsilon_Bq=\varepsilon$, and $S_Bq=qS$. In particular $b_a=q(e_a)$ satisfies $\Delta_B(b_a)=b_a\otimes b_a$, $\varepsilon_B(b_a)=1$, $S_B(b_a)=b_{-a}$ and $b_ab_c=b_{a+c}$.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(c), subgroup part, pp.233-234; Theorem 12.8; Hopf compatibility expanded

proof.text: Let $M$ be the image of the homomorphism $\mathbf Z^r\to B^\times$, $a\mapsto b_a$, where $b_a^{-1}=b_{-a}$. It is an abelian group, written additively, generated by the images of the $r$ standard basis vectors; hence it is finitely generated, even when $r=0$. For $m\in M$ let $u_m\in B^\times$ be its underlying unit. These are pairwise distinct elements of $B$, all group-like by Step 1. Surjectivity of $q$ shows that they span $B$: write a preimage as a finite sum $\sum_a c_a e_a$ and group together terms having equal $b_a$.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(c), subgroup proof, p.234; explicit image group for Theorem 12.8

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-coalgebra-group-like-independent] to the coalgebra $B$ from Step 1. Its hypotheses hold over the field $F$, without a reducedness or finite-dimensionality assumption. It says that the distinct $u_m$ are linearly independent. Together with the spanning calculation in Step 2 this makes $(u_m)_{m\in M}$ an $F$-basis of $B$.

Define $\theta:F[M]\to B$ by $\theta(\sum_m c_m e_m)=\sum_m c_m u_m$. Step 3 gives bijectivity, and $u_0=1$, $u_{m+n}=u_mu_n$ give multiplicativity and preservation of the unit by finite distributivity. Step 1 gives $\Delta_B\theta(e_m)=u_m\otimes u_m=(\theta\otimes\theta)\Delta(e_m)$, $\varepsilon_B\theta(e_m)=1$ and $S_B\theta(e_m)=u_{-m}=\theta S(e_m)$; linearity extends these equalities to all finite sums. Thus $\theta$ is an isomorphism with exactly the required Hopf operations. The contravariant spectrum correspondence [def-weil-affine-spectrum] gives the scheme isomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\theta:K\to\operatorname{Spec}F[M]$. Both $F[M]$ and $B$ are commutative Hopf $F$-algebras (Step 1 and [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]), and $\theta$ preserves the three operations, so by [lem-sfb-hopf-spectrum-functor] $\operatorname{Spec}\theta$ is a group-scheme homomorphism, the group laws being those induced by the Hopf operations; for $K$ this is its own group law because $\Delta_B,\varepsilon_B,S_B$ are the pullbacks of its multiplication, identity and inverse. Its inverse is $\operatorname{Spec}\theta^{-1}$, and $\theta^{-1}$ also preserves the three operations, so $K\simeq D(M)$ as $F$-group schemes. Here [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] identifies the product schemes with the spectra of the tensor algebras, so the comultiplication identity is precisely compatibility with multiplication.

source.place: Theorem 12.8, p.233; basis isomorphism and Hopf compatibility expanded

proof.text: If $B$ has finite dimension $d$, then $M$ has at most $d$ elements: otherwise choose $d+1$ distinct elements of $M$. Their $u_m$ form an independent family by Step 3, contrary to [lem-weil-independent-family-card-le-dimension], which bounds its size by $d$. Hence $M$ is finite. Since $F$ is already algebraically closed, the diagonalizable description just constructed is also the required description after extension to an algebraic closure, proving the multiplicative-type assertion. No step used smoothness, reducedness, or a restriction on the characteristic or on the order of $K$.

source.place: Theorem 12.8 and Definition 12.17, pp.233 and 236; finite-dimensional consequence of the displayed basis

proof_origin.place: Theorem 12.9(c), subgroup proof, p.234, and Theorem 12.8, p.233, using Proposition 4.23, p.93; image-group construction and finite-dimensional consequence expanded.
